title: Data Handling
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Data Handling. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Bar, pictograph, line and circle graphs
Questioning samples, scale and misleading displays

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
From question to data

Decide what variable is being measured, who or what is included, and whether values are categories or numerical measurements. A sample should represent the population fairly; convenience samples can bias conclusions.

Organising and displaying

Tally and frequency tables count observations. Bar graphs compare categories; line graphs show change across an ordered scale such as time; pictographs use a key; circle graphs show parts of a whole. Choose a display that matches the data and label axes, units and scale.

Summaries and chance

Mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent value. Range describes the full spread. For equally likely outcomes, probability is (\(favourable outcomes/total outcomes\)).

Worked example: For scores (\(2,3,3,7,10\)), mean is 5, median is 3, mode is 3 and range is 8. The high score affects the mean more than the median.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Read graph keys and scales before interpreting visual height or area.
  • Sort data before finding the median and state how an even count is handled.
  • Use a frequency table to avoid recounting raw observations.
  • Ask who was excluded from the sample and whether the sample is representative.
  • Compare the mean and median when data contain outliers.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Mean = total of values divided by number of observations.
  • Median is the middle ordered value, or mean of two middle values for an even count.
  • Probability lies from 0 to 1; impossible = 0 and certain = 1.
  • A fair graph needs clear labels, consistent intervals and an honest baseline.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    A pictograph uses one book symbol for 4 books. How many books do 5 symbols represent?

    1. (\(9\))
    2. (\(16\))
    3. (\(20\))
    4. (\(25\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(20\))

    Multiply symbols by the key value: (\(5\cdot4=20\)) books.

  2. Core:

    A data set is (\(2,3,3,5,7\)). What is its mode?

    1. (\(2\))
    2. (\(3\))
    3. (\(5\))
    4. (\(7\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(3\))

    The value 3 appears twice; each other value appears once. The mode is 3.

  3. Foundation:

    Find the median of (\(3, 5, 8, 10, 14\)).

    1. (\(5\))
    2. (\(8\))
    3. (\(9\))
    4. (\(10\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(8\))

    The five ordered observations have middle value 8.

  4. Standard:

    A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling an even number?

    1. (\(1/6\))
    2. (\(1/3\))
    3. (\(1/2\))
    4. (\(2/3\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1/2\))

    Even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6: (\(3/6=1/2\)).

  5. Challenge:

    Which measure is usually least affected by one extremely high observation?

    1. Mean
    2. Median
    3. Range
    4. Maximum
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Median

    The median depends on the middle position in ordered data and is generally more resistant to an extreme value than the mean.
